question: What makes an item qualify as a medical sharp?

options.A: It has a sharp point or edge capable of cutting skin
options.B: It must be sterilized after every single patient use
options.C: It is made entirely of hard stainless steel
options.D: It is used exclusively for surgical operations in theatre

explanation: You've got this! Sharps are simply any medical items that can puncture, cut, or scratch the skin. Knowing this helps keep you and your patients safe on the ward. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h1)

question: Which of these everyday ward items is considered a medical sharp?
explanation: Nice try if you missed it! Broken glass can easily cut the skin, so we treat it just like a needle and dispose of it in a sharps container. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h1)

question: Which bloodborne infection has the highest risk of spreading after just one accidental needle-stick injury?
explanation: Don't worry, this is a tricky clinical fact! Hepatitis B is very resilient and has a much higher transmission rate per needle-stick than HIV or Hep C. This is why getting your Hep B vaccine as a nursing student is super important! [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h2)

question: Why does a hollow-bore needle (like a syringe needle) carry a higher infection risk than a solid suture needle?

options.A: It contains a lumen that can trap and transfer infected blood
options.B: It is always longer than standard surgical suture needles
options.C: It remains inside the patient's body for a longer duration
options.D: It is manufactured using cheaper, more porous metal alloys

explanation: Think of a hollow needle like a tiny straw—it actually holds a small amount of blood inside (the lumen), which gets carried right into the skin if an accident happens. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h2)

question: What is the safest way to recap a needle if you absolutely have to do it?

options.A: Holding the cap firmly with the second hand
options.B: Pushing the needle directly into the cap using fingers
options.D: Bending the needle against the table to secure the cap

explanation: Great job! The one-handed scoop method is a lifesaver because it keeps your free hand safely away from the pointy end. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h3)

question: You just finished giving an injection on the ward. What is the very next thing you should do with the used syringe and needle?

options.A: Remove the needle by hand before throwing the syringe in the bin
options.B: Recap the needle using both hands before carrying it to the utility room
options.C: Place the uncapped syringe on the bedside table for later disposal
options.D: Drop the syringe and needle directly into a nearby sharps container

explanation: Spot on! Never try to detach or recap needles by hand. Drop the whole syringe and needle unit straight into the sharps box right away. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h3)

question: At what point should a sharps container be safely closed and replaced?
explanation: Good to know! We stop at the three-quarters mark (the fill line) so that no needles poke out or cause accidental injuries when people handle the box. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h4)

question: Where is the best place to put a sharps container in a treatment or injection room?

options.A: High up on a top shelf to keep it out of patient reach
options.B: On the floor in the corner away from the patient bed
options.C: Within arm's reach and at eye level near the point of use
options.D: Inside a locked floor cabinet beneath the medication trolley

explanation: You got it! Keeping the sharps box close by means you never have to walk across a busy room carrying an exposed needle. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h4)

question: What is the very first thing you must do if you accidentally suffer a needle-stick injury?

options.A: Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and running water
options.B: Fill out an incident report form in the nursing office
options.C: Suck the puncture site vigorously to remove bad blood
options.D: Apply a strong antiseptic solution like pure bleach

explanation: Always remember: soap, running water, and gentle washing come first! This washes away surface germs before they can settle in. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h5)

question: When washing a fresh needle-stick wound, why should you avoid scrubbing it aggressively?

options.A: It can damage delicate skin tissues and increase pathogen absorption
options.B: It inactivates the antiseptic properties of standard hand soap
options.C: It prevents the hospital management from investigating the accident
options.D: It causes the wound to bleed too much to apply a plaster

explanation: It's counterintuitive, but scrubbing too hard actually creates tiny new cuts that let germs get deeper into your bloodstream. Gentle washing is always best! [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h5)
